The Call of Cthulhu. H.P. Lovecraft's 1928 novella introduces Cthulhu, an ancient cosmic entity sleeping beneath the Pacific Ocean, and establishes the tradition of cosmic horror—the terror that arises not from personal evil but from humanity's insignificance in a universe ruled by indifferent, ancient powers. The narrative is framed as a scholar piecing together fragmented accounts that reveal a global cult devoted to an entity that threatens both human sanity and civilization.

A protagonist discovers documents and relics suggesting a worldwide religion devoted to Cthulhu, a sleeping god imprisoned beneath the sea. Cthulhu is an immense entity—part octopus, part dragon, part humanoid—whose very appearance can drive humans to madness or death. The story incorporates the Necronomicon, a fictional grimoire of occult knowledge that Lovecraft reused across his fiction, establishing an interconnected universe of cosmic terror. A cult called the Order of Dagon has performed rituals and sacrifices across continents in service to Cthulhu's eventual awakening.

Lovecraft uses a framing device of discovered journals and reports to create verisimilitude, blending academic discourse with mounting dread. He establishes the subgenre of cosmic horror itself: terror derived not from evil human action but from encounters with entities whose nature is fundamentally incomprehensible and hostile to human existence. The Call of Cthulhu became the founding text of Lovecraftian fiction, inspiring countless writers and entire shared fictional universes. It remains the source text for the interconnected Lovecraft mythos and the Necronomicon, the fictional grimoire that anchors his entire body of work.
